sources.title: Modern Defense Guide and overview (search snippets only)

overview: Black plays 1...g6 and 2...Bg7 and lets White build the e4-d4 centre, delaying ...Nf6 (which separates it from the Pirc), then attacks the centre with ...c5, ...e5 or ...Nc6 and the pressure of the g7 bishop. It is a simple, repeatable set-up that Black can adopt against almost anything, and its flexible move order makes it a practical surprise weapon. White's main tries are the Standard line (2.d4 Bg7 3.Nc3 d6 4.f4 or 3.Nf3), the Averbakh-style 2.c4 / 2.Nc3 set-ups, and c3 to blunt the g7 bishop; White often attacks on the kingside with f4, while Black seeks counterplay against an over-extended centre. Sources call it sound but with a risk of passivity or of letting White build an overwhelming centre; it is moderately popular (about 1.7% of games in 2025 on one database) with occasional master use (Suttles, Davies, McNab, Carlsen).

white_ideas.idea: Take the broad centre (e4, d4, c4 or f4) and use the space for a kingside attack, usually with f4.
Blunt the g7 bishop with c3 or play the Averbakh set-up (c4, Nc3) to reach Pirc-like or Maroczy-like positions.
Exploit Black's delayed ...Nf6 by building the centre quickly, for example Monkey's Bum Deferred with early Bc4 and Qf3.

black_ideas.idea: Fianchetto the bishop to g7, make waiting moves and strike at the centre with ...c5, ...e5 or ...Nc6 when White commits.
Delay ...Nf6 to keep flexibility and the option of transposing to Pirc, Philidor or other structures.
Queenside counterplay with ...a6/...b5 or ...c6 and ...Bg4 in the Standard line.

typical_structures.structure: Black pawns on d6, e7 and g6 with a bishop on g7; White holds e4, d4 and often c4 or f4 (a broad centre).
Pirc-style or Maroczy-like structures when c4/Nc3 reach the Averbakh set-up (the subtree includes 1.d4 g6 2.c4 Bg7 3.Nc3 d6).
Standard line with f4: Black c6 and ...Bg4 pressure on White's overextended centre.

character.notes: Chessiverse labels it 'solid and balanced' (s2); Wikipedia calls it sound but risking passivity if Black is careless, and says White can generate real attacking chances (e.g. Monkey's Bum Deferred) (s1). The set-up is slow and flexible: White usually gets space and the attack, Black waits and counters. Risk: allowing White to build 'an overwhelming centre' (s2). Typical play is plan-based rather than forcing. Leaning balanced to solid.

gambit.notes: No gambit at the root. Sidelines exist where White offers a pawn but none are central.

soundness.notes: Sound. Wikipedia: considered sound, though precise play is required (s1). Statistics from a large database are essentially balanced (White 49.4%, Black 46.2%, 38.1 million games, all ratings, not an engine verdict) (s2). No source claims it is refuted. Not Dubious.

structure.notes: White keeps a big pawn centre and Black allows it, then challenges with a pawn break. The centre is typically tense and often semi-closed until ...c5/...e5; later pawns can come off for an open game. The sources do not label it, so my reading is: tense centre, closed-leaning (my own understanding, unsourced).

approach.notes: A repeatable set-up: Black 'follows a simple, repeatable set-up rather than a forcing line' (s3 snippet) and can play ...g6/...Bg7/...d6 against many first moves (the subtree includes 1.d4 g6 2.c4 Bg7 3.Nc3 d6). That fits a System. Frequency is modest (1.71% of games in 2025, s2) and master use is occasional but includes Carlsen, Suttles and Davies (s1, s2), so not Offbeat.

level.notes: Judged for Black. Chessiverse: 'accessible across all skill levels', emphasising strategic understanding over memorisation; theory adherence is 78.7% at 1200 Elo versus 92.1% at 2500 (s2). Wikipedia: moderate theory (s1). The skill is in knowing when and how to hit the centre and avoiding passivity. Intermediate rather than Beginner (my own judgment: a good first repertoire needs clear plans, and the Modern needs timing judgment).

sublines_that_differ.name: Standard line
sublines_that_differ.how: White's f4 centre against Black's ...c6 and ...Bg4, sharper than the quiet Nf3 lines.

sublines_that_differ.name: Averbakh / Maroczy-style
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 g6 2. c4 Bg7 3. Nc3 d6 (also reached from 1.d4 g6)
sublines_that_differ.how: Pirc and King's Indian-like structures with c4; quiet, positional.

sublines_that_differ.name: Monkey's Bum Deferred
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 g6 2. d4 Bg7 3. Nc3 c6 4. Bc4 (or similar) with Qf3
sublines_that_differ.how: Early Bc4 and Qf3 for White, a more aggressive set-up.

sublines_that_differ.name: 3.c3 / blunting the bishop
sublines_that_differ.how: White blunts the g7 bishop and builds a solid centre; quiet.

description.claim: The Modern Defense is a dynamic and highly flexible hypermodern system where Black invites White to build a large pawn centre and challenges it from the flanks.
description.note: Matches the standard description; 'dynamic' is arguable, as Chessiverse says solid and balanced.

description.claim: The core idea is to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop to g7, creating a long-range piece that fuels counterattacks.
description.note: Bg7 pressing the centre is the central idea.

description.claim: It is perfect for creative, independent-minded players who enjoy unbalanced positions and understand strategic plans rather than long forced variations.

common_plans.claim: Black: fianchetto the king's bishop, cede the centre temporarily, and then attack it with pawn breaks like ...c5 or ...e5.
White: seize a space advantage with a large pawn centre (e.g. d4, c4) and use it to develop pieces and launch an attack.
common_plans.note: Broad centre and a kingside attack with f4 are named.

common_plans.claim: Black: create counterplay on the queenside with moves like ...a6 and ...b5, or directly challenge White's king.
common_plans.note: Queenside play is plausible (my own understanding) but the sources read mention ...c5, ...e5 and ...c6 more than ...a6/...b5.

common_plans.claim: White: restrict the power of the g7 bishop and challenge Black's kingside structure, often with an h-pawn push.
common_plans.note: Restricting the g7 bishop (c3) is supported; the h-pawn push is not mentioned in the sources read, though h4-h5 does occur in lines (own understanding).
